recipe.history:
Blue cheese is among the most ancient of intentional fermentations, with origins reaching back to the cave-aged cheeses of medieval Europe. The most famous of all, Roquefort, is said to have been discovered by a young French shepherd who left his lunch of bread and fresh cheese in the Combalou caves of southern France and returned weeks later to find it transformed — the cool, moist cave air and naturally occurring Penicillium roqueforti mold had threaded the cheese with veins of blue-green brilliance. By the fourteenth century, Roquefort had royal patronage; Charles VI granted a monopoly on its production to the village of Roquefort-sur-Soulzon in 1411. Gorgonzola of Italy and Stilton of England followed as the great blue cheese trinity of Europe, each a product of specific microbial terroir, each pungent and funky and alive with flavor in a way that mild cheeses simply are not. Blue cheese is the cheese of the brave and the curious — it demands something of the eater, and it rewards that courage generously.

Blue cheese arrived in American cuisine primarily through the influence of mid-twentieth century food culture — it appeared on steakhouse salads, stuffed into celery, crumbled over wedge salads at every supper club from New York to Los Angeles. The burger application came later, accelerated by the gourmet burger boom of the 1990s when restaurants began treating the hamburger as a canvas for serious flavor rather than a vehicle for mere sustenance. Blue cheese's pungent depth proved to be a revelatory counterpoint to the charred, fatty richness of a beef patty — the salt and funk of the cheese amplifying the beef's savoriness while cutting through its fat. Paired with beet ketchup, whose earthy sweetness plays against the blue cheese's sharpness, and crispy fried onion strings that add textural percussion, the blue cheese burger became a fixture of any serious burger menu. Gene Belcher, that magnificent, music-obsessed food enthusiast from the Belcher family, would undoubtedly approve of a burger this bold and unapologetic in its flavors.

I made this burger for the first time on a rainy Tuesday, the kind of day that calls for something deeply savory and a little bit funky. I had a wedge of Gorgonzola dolce in the cheese drawer and a bunch of beets I had been meaning to roast for days. I roasted the beets until they were tender and sweet, blended them into a ketchup with apple cider vinegar and brown sugar and a little smoked paprika, and the result was so deeply, earthily beautiful that I stood there tasting it off a spoon long after I should have moved on to the onion strings. The fried onion strings came out in crackling, golden tangles, shattering satisfyingly against the soft bun. When I assembled everything — the funky Gorgonzola crumbled over the rosy patty, the dark jewel-red beet ketchup, the crackling onion strings — it felt like a performance, like something that had a rhythm and a groove to it. Gene would have composed a jingle about it on the spot, and it would have been a banger.

To cook a burger to anything beyond medium rare is, philosophically speaking, an act of willful ignorance about what meat is and what it wants to become. A burger cooked to 130–135°F (54–57°C) is a burger that still contains all of its natural moisture and intramuscular fat in liquid, basting form. The crust sears hard and brown and Maillard-complex on the outside, but the interior remains rosy and yielding — a study in contrasts that mirrors the contrast of funky blue cheese against sweet beet ketchup. Every element of this burger is about counterpoint, about tension and resolution, about the unexpected harmony that emerges when bold, seemingly incompatible flavors meet. A medium rare patty is the bass line holding all of that together — remove it, cook it gray and dry, and the whole composition falls apart.
ingredients: 1 large egg plus 1 egg for egg wash
3 tbsp sesame seeds (black and white mixed)
For the funky blue cheese crumble:
6 oz Gorgonzola dolce (or creamy domestic blue cheese)
3 medium red beets, roasted, peeled, and roughly chopped
1 large yellow onion, sliced into thin rings
Neutral oil for frying (about 2 inches deep in a heavy pot)
2 cups baby spinach or mixed greens
instructions: 1. Make the sesame buns: Combine yeast, warm water, and sugar; let sit 5–10 minutes until foamy. Mix flour and salt in a stand mixer bowl. Add yeast mixture, softened butter, and one egg. Knead with dough hook on medium 8 minutes until smooth and elastic.

2. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover, and let rise 1–1.5 hours until doubled. Punch down, divide into 6 portions, and shape into tight rounds. Place on parchment-lined baking sheet, cover, and proof 45 minutes until puffy.
3. Beat remaining egg with 1 tbsp water. Brush bun tops with egg wash and press sesame seeds liberally onto the surface. Bake at 375°F for 16–18 minutes until deep golden. Cool completely.

4. Make the beet ketchup: Preheat oven to 400°F. Wrap beets individually in foil and roast 50–60 minutes until fork-tender. Cool, peel, and roughly chop. Blend roasted beets, apple cider vinegar, brown sugar, smoked paprika, garlic powder, salt, and a splash of water in a blender or food processor until completely smooth. Adjust seasoning. Refrigerate until needed.

5. Make the blue cheese crumble: Combine Gorgonzola with heavy cream and cracked pepper. Mash lightly with a fork until it forms a cohesive but still chunky spreadable mixture. Refrigerate until assembling.

6. Make the crispy onion strings: Soak onion rings in buttermilk for at least 30 minutes. In a bowl, whisk together flour, smoked paprika, garlic powder, cayenne, and salt. Working in batches, lift onion rings from buttermilk, let excess drip off, and dredge in seasoned flour, pressing to adhere.

7. Heat 2 inches of neutral oil in a heavy-bottomed pot to 365°F. Fry onion strings in batches 2–3 minutes until golden and crispy. Drain on a wire rack lined with paper towels. Season immediately with a pinch of salt.

8. Prepare the patties: Divide ground beef into 6 portions (about 4 oz each). Form gently into patties 3/4 inch thick with a dimple in the center. Season both sides with salt and pepper. Refrigerate 15 minutes.

9. Cook the patties: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add neutral oil. Sear patties dimple-side up 3 minutes until a hard, dark crust forms. Flip and cook 2–3 minutes more until internal temperature reads 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Rest 3–4 minutes, tented with foil.
10. Toast the buns cut-side down in a dry skillet over medium heat 1–2 minutes until golden.

11. Assemble: Spread a generous spoonful of beet ketchup on the bottom bun. Place the rested patty on top. Spoon or crumble a generous portion of blue cheese mixture over the hot patty so it melts and softens slightly. Pile a tangle of crispy onion strings on top. Add a few leaves of dressed spinach. Crown with the top bun. Serve immediately while onion strings are still crisp.
